analysis.one_liner: Requires companies to notify consumers and let them block sales of their personal data.
analysis.headline: The bill won 5 cosponsors from both parties but never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required any company handling personal information on more than 5,000 consumers to post a plain-language privacy policy, notify customers before using their data for unrelated purposes, let people opt out for five years of having their data sold to outside companies, and maintain a security plan to prevent data breaches. The Federal Trade Commission could enforce violations with doubled civil penalties. At the same time, the bill would have let companies comply through FTC-approved self-regulatory programs instead of direct enforcement, capped penalties at $500,000 no matter how many consumers were affected, barred consumers from suing on their own, and wiped out state privacy laws across the country.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers would gain a national baseline they do not have under general law: a right to see a plain-language privacy policy, to be told before their data is used for unrelated purposes, and to block for five years the sale of their information to outside companies. The FTC would gain an explicit enforcement tool with doubled civil penalties.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers who share data with companies

how_it_helps.text: Companies handling personal data on more than 5,000 consumers must give notice before using that data for purposes unrelated to the transaction it was collected for, and must post a plain-language privacy policy [S2][S3].

Consumers get a free, five-year opportunity to preclude the sale or disclosure of their personal information to companies outside the collector's corporate family, and companies cannot ask them to reconsider for at least a year [S3].
Each covered entity must implement an information security policy designed to prevent unauthorized disclosure, approved by senior management and with a designated security officer [S3].
A violation is an unfair or deceptive practice under the FTC Act with civil penalties doubled, enforced by the Federal Trade Commission [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies in the data and online marketing economy bear the compliance costs of notices, opt-out systems, security programs, and possible FTC-approved self-regulatory memberships. Consumers bear a subtler cost: their state's privacy laws would be overridden, and the bill's self-regulatory safe harbor, $500,000 penalty cap, and ban on private lawsuits would keep enforcement light even where data abuse affects millions of people.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state privacy laws, wiping out any stricter protections states such as California had adopted, and bars states from enforcing the federal rules [S3].

Companies that join an FTC-approved self-regulatory program are presumed compliant and cannot be fined for violations unless they willfully defy the program's rules, shifting policing to industry-run bodies with self-certification [S3].
Civil penalties are capped at $500,000 for all related violations by a single violator, no matter how many consumers were affected or how long the violations lasted [S3].
The bill explicitly provides no private right of action, so consumers could not sue companies that misuse their data even under state law [S3].
The bill's definition of 'transaction' includes a company marketing its own products to its own customers, so everyday advertising use of collected data would not trigger the notice requirement [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's notice and opt-out rights are real but modest, and a consumer would have to notice and use them without any help from a private lawsuit. What the bill takes away is larger in some states: national preemption would replace stricter state privacy rules with a floor built around industry self-regulation, a low penalty cap, and no right to sue. An honest supporter would call this a workable first national privacy standard; an honest critic would call it a ceiling designed to be lower than the state laws it displaces.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, then to a subcommittee two weeks later, and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 13, 2011 by Rep. Cliff Stearns with cosponsors Reps. Matheson, Bilbray, and Manzullo, and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1][S3][S5].
On April 25, 2011 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade, and no further action was taken for the rest of the 112th Congress [S4][S5].
The bill never reached the House floor or the Senate, so no national consumer privacy standard and no preemption of state privacy laws resulted from it [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that collect, sell, and market personal data: they faced no new federal obligations, and the stronger state privacy laws on the books remained in force only as scattered patchwork rather than being replaced by either a stronger or weaker national rule.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, for a total of 5 cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan, a Republican sponsor with 2 Democratic and 3 Republican cosponsors, but the bill died in committee without any vote, so no party split on the merits was ever recorded [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Data brokers and online advertising companies
industries.note: The bill would have kept the market for consumer data intact, requiring only notice and an opt-out for sales to outside companies while counting a company's own marketing as an exempt 'transaction'. It would have locked this system in nationally by preempting stricter state privacy laws, while adding real compliance and penalty costs.

industries.industry: Self-regulatory and seal programs (industry privacy groups)
industries.note: The bill creates FTC-approved self-regulatory programs whose members are presumed compliant and shielded from civil penalties absent willful noncompliance, making industry-run policing the main enforcement channel. Consumer disputes would be routed first through these programs' own processes.

industries.industry: Online retailers and consumer-facing web companies
industries.note: They would bear the costs of notices, opt-out mechanics, and security policies covering anyone handling data on more than 5,000 consumers, but would gain in exchange a single national rule instead of fifty state standards.
